Two weeks into the latest round of fighting, the US and Iran are trading calibrated strikes while Trump talks about a “massive attack” big enough to force a peace deal.

CENTCOM has now logged 13 consecutive nights of strikes on Iranian military targets around the Strait of Hormuz, officially to “degrade” Iran’s ability to threaten commercial shipping. 

Iran answers by hitting US bases and allied facilities in Kuwait and Bahrain, and by having the Revolutionary Guard declare Hormuz “closed” while tankers creep through under escort. 

In parallel, Yemen’s Houthi militants — Iran’s Axis of Resistance franchise — claim drone and missile strikes on Saudi tankers in the Red Sea and announce a blockade on Saudi shipping through Bab el‑Mandeb, turning a second narrow channel into a risk point.

Trump tells Axios he’s “close to making a decision” on attacks “bigger than ever before,” says Iran “hasn’t received enough pain yet,” and posts on Truth Social that any damage to ships or cargo “will be paid for by Iranian money” frozen under US control.

At the same time, Trump threatens to destroy “one bridge or power plant” every time Iran hits shipping, while Tehran warns that if he does, it will escalate against regional energy infrastructure.

The result is a war that the White House insists is limited while it quietly pushes every maritime chokepoint closer to crisis. Hormuz, which used to carry about a fifth of global energy flows, has slowed to a trickle. 

Bab el‑Mandeb is now partially avoided after the Houthi blockade announcement, even as Chinese‑owned tankers test the route under risk. 

Oil sits above $100, gas above $4, and Trump — who last month cited the risk of a global economic crash as a reason to accept a truce — is back to promising “major military punishment” against Iran and the Houthis if they touch commercial ships.

The oddest part is the rhetoric: “peace deal” via threats to blow up bridges and power plants, “security of shipping” via nightly airstrikes, “compensation” via raiding frozen assets.

⚡️ More than 1.7 million Iranians register for Arbaeen pilgrimage, data shows

📌 Tehran, IRNA – Over 1.7 million Iranians have registered to take part in the Arbaeen pilgrimage, according to the latest figures.

The statistics released on Friday show that 58 percent of those registered are men and 42 percent are women, with Tehran, Razavi Khorasan and Khuzestan provinces recording the highest numbers of applicants.
​
Of those registered, 58 percent have selected the Mehran border crossing, 24 percent have chosen Shalamcheh, while 11 percent and four percent have selected Khosravi and Chazzabeh border crossings, respectively. Two percent of those registered have also chosen air travel to go to Iraq for the Arbaeen pilgrimage.
​
Arbaeen marks the 40th day after Ashura, which commemorates the martyrdom of Imam Hossein (PBUH), the third Shia Imam.
​
Every year, millions of pilgrims from Iran and other Muslim countries travel to Iraq to take part in the annual Arbaeen pilgrimage, many of them making the journey on foot to the holy city of Karbala, home to the shrine of Imam Hossein (PBUH).
​
Recently, Iran’s Minister of Roads and Urban Development Farzaneh Sadegh and her Iraqi counterpart have reviewed the latest status of the Shalamcheh–Basra railway project, the road transport agreement, as well as coordination to facilitate Arbaeen 2026 travel.

💬 Iran tells UN US attack on rescue vessels constitutes ‘war crime’

📌 New York, IRNA – Iran has formally complained to the United Nations, saying the United States has committed a “war crime” by deliberately targeting two Iranian maritime search-and-rescue vessels, saying the ships were engaged solely in humanitarian operations and were not involved in any military activity at the time of the attack.

In a letter addressed to UN Secretary-General António Guterres and the president of the UN Security Council, Gholamhossein Darzi, Iran’s ambassador and deputy permanent representative to the United Nations, said the US attacked the Iranian rescue vessels Naji-15 and Naji-16 during the early hours of July 23 while they were operating in Iran’s territorial waters off Hormozgan Province.
​
Darzi said the two vessels were dedicated exclusively to maritime search-and-rescue missions and were protected under international humanitarian law and the law of the sea.
​
The following is the full text of the letter:
​
Upon instructions from my Government and further to our previous letters, including the letters dated 16, 17 and 20 July 2026, concerning the continued acts of aggression and grave violations of international law committed by the United States of America against the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Islamic Republic of Iran, I wish to draw your urgent attention, and that of the members of the Security Council, to yet another serious violation of international humanitarian law committed by the United States against humanitarian maritime search and rescue assets of the Islamic Republic of Iran.
​
In the early hours of 23 July 2026, the United States deliberately attacked two Iranian maritime search and rescue (SAR) vessels, Naji-15 and Naji-16, operating in the territorial waters of the Islamic Republic of Iran in Hormozgan Province. According to the competent Iranian maritime authorities, the vessels were engaged exclusively in humanitarian search and rescue operations and sustained significant damage as a result of the attack. This was not an isolated incident. Since the commencement of the United States' and the Israeli regime's aggression against the Islamic Republic of Iran on 28 February 2026, Iranian search and rescue vessels and sea ambulances engaged solely in life-saving humanitarian missions have repeatedly been targeted, revealing a disturbing pattern of deliberate attacks against protected humanitarian assets.
​
The deliberate targeting of vessels assigned exclusively to maritime search and rescue operations constitutes a grave violation of international humanitarian law and international maritime law. Search and rescue vessels perform an exclusively humanitarian function by saving the lives of persons in distress at sea. Article 27 of the Second Geneva Convention of 1949 requires that small crafts employed by States or officially recognized rescue institutions for coastal rescue operations be respected and protected. The vessels Naji-15 and Naji-16 fall within the scope of this protection and were not engaged in any military activity or direct participation in hostilities. Their intentional targeting therefore constitutes a serious violation of international humanitarian law and amounts to a war crime.
​
By deliberately targeting humanitarian search and rescue assets, the United States has not only endangered the lives of rescue personnel, but has also placed at risk all mariners in distress, regardless of their nationality. Such conduct strikes at the very foundation of the international legal framework established to safeguard humanitarian operations and ensure the safety of navigation at sea.
